articles.title: Ranking WWE's 10 Greatest Forgotten Fall Classics
articles.summary: The Fall months in WWE have long been considered the doldrums of the pro wrestling calendar; a season in which the company bides time before heating up the product in time for the march to WrestleMania.
articles.body:
The Fall months in WWE have long been considered the doldrums of the pro wrestling calendar; a season in which the company bides time before heating up the product in time for the march to WrestleMania.

While that may be the perception, the period between September and November has produced its fair share of forgotten classics.

Relive those hidden gems from WWE's "lull" season and find out why they deserve your attention.

Why Isn't The First Hell in a Cell Included?

Shawn Michaels and The Undertaker made history with the incredible debut of Hell in a Cell at In Your House: Bad Blood in October of 1997.

The match was extraordinary, a bloody, violent affair the likes of which that match was made for. It also featured the shocking, unforgettable debut of Kane, kicking off a sibling rivalry story that would captivate fans and go on to become one of the greatest arcs in WWE history.

It is appropriately ranked among the best matches in company history, as well as one of the most influential and important.

For that reason, it cannot justifiably be considered one a hidden gem and thus, misses out on inclusion on this list.

It is, however, hands-down the best match to ever take place in the Fall months in WWE.

Honorable Mention: The Rock vs. Kurt Angle (No Mercy 2000)

Lost in the chaotic game of championship hot potato that ensued in 2000 was the excellent match-up between The Rock and Kurt Angle that headlined that year's No Mercy pay-per-view.

The Great One and the Olympic gold medalist had demonstrated their in-ring chemistry in previous matches, but had not yet had the opportunity to deliver in a marquee spot.

A back and forth contest that proved to even the biggest doubters that Angle was ready to thrive at the top of the card, it culminated in typical Attitude Era fashion, with chicanery in the form of McMahon interference.

First, Stephanie ate a Rock Bottom, which brought Triple H out. The Cerebral Assassin dropped his longtime rival with a Pedigree and carried his wife to safety.

Then, late in the bout, Rikishi arrived on the scene with a sledgehammer, hellbent on assisting his cousin to a championship win. Instead, he blasted him by accident and the Olympian delivered an Angle Slam to win the match and the first of four WWE titles.

10. Matt Hardy vs. Edge (Unforgiven 2005)

The intensely personal rivalry between Matt Hardy and Edge, which began with the latter's shocking affair with Lita off-screen, bled over onto WWE television in 2005. Following an unsatisfying conclusion to their first match-up at SummerSlam that August, they kicked off the Fall with a battle inside a steel cage at Unforgiven that not only stole that particular show, but set the bar remarkably high for the rest of the year.

A physical battle that built and built before culminating in a jaw-dropping leg drop from Hardy from the top of the cage, it gave the audience exactly what it wanted from the latest in their heated rivalry.

More importantly, it provided Hardy with a moment of both revenge and redemption, arguably one of the best in his career as a singles competitor.

There is plenty to be said of the follow-up and, ultimately, how Hardy was done dirty in the aftermath of the victory. For one night in Oklahoma City, though, he looked like a breakout main event star ready to move on from the heartache caused by the dissolution of his relationship onto bigger things.

9. The Undertaker vs. Shawn Michaels (In Your House: Ground Zero)

While the iconic first Hell in a Cell match may not be eligible for this list due to its proper ranking as one of the best in WWE history, the first encounter between The Undertaker and Shawn Michaels from the previous month's In Your House: Ground Zero more than deserves recognition among forgotten Fall classics.

The Heartbreak Kid wanted nothing to do with The Deadman after costing him the WWE Championship at SummerSlam, then undergoing a heel turn and joining forces with Hunter Hearst Helmsley and Chyna to beat him down in subsequent weeks.

A true cowardly villain, he attempted to evade the Phenom at points throughout the match before it devolved into a wild and chaotic brawl that concluded in unsatisfying fashion when Tim White called for the bell and declared the match a no-contest.

While that may not have been an ideal outcome, the brawl that spilled out of the ring and into the arena set the stage for the much-needed steel confines of the aforementioned Hell in a Cell Match.

Michaels and Undertaker took the WWE fans on a ride and necessitated an even greater, historically relevant match that just so happened to cast an enormous shadow of their first wild, chaotic, hella fun showdown.

8. Edge and Rey Mysterio vs. Kurt Angle and Chris Benoit (SmackDown, November 7, 2002)

Edge and Rey Mysterio fell just shy of becoming the first WWE Tag Team Champions, losing to Kurt Angle and Chris Benoit in a tournament final at No Mercy 2002.

Looking to get their win back and to relieve their rivals of the gold, Edge and Mysterio battled Angle and Benoit in a Best 2-Out-of-3 Falls Match on the November 7 episode of SmackDown.

A match that, arguably, eclipsed their instant classic from pay-per-view just weeks earlier, it captivated the audience and concluded with the babyfaces capturing the gold.

Forgotten today largely due to the understandable erasure of Benoit from WWE history, it was a brilliant match featuring four Superstars in peak form. It was also another entry in the SmackDown Six story, which also featured Eddie and Chavo Guerrero, and dominated the blue brand in the criminally short run of Paul Heyman as the lead creative force behind the scenes.

John Cena and Edge had several classic encounters over the course of their legendary rivalry, with none more overrated than the main event of the Unforgiven 2006 pay-per-view.

That may strike a nerve with some, but that does not make it any less true.

With that said, it is still an excellent match that more than deserves placement on this list.

A match that featured a greatest hits assortment of spots, coupled with a few original ideas sprinkled in for good measure, and an all-timer finish that saw Cena deliver an Attitude Adjustment from the top of a ladder, it was head and shoulders above the second half of the year.

The Last Man Standing Match between the two in April of 2009 was a better match, but the historical implications of the match and what it meant to Cena and Edge's respective runs as main event talent earns it the reputation that it has.

6. The Undertaker vs. Brock Lesnar (No Mercy 2002)

Since they first clashed inside Hell in a Cell at No Mercy 2002, The Undertaker and Brock Lesnar have wrestled countless times, including the infamous WrestleMania 30 match that saw The Beast end The Deadman's iconic unbeaten streak at the Showcase of the Immortals.

That match in the Fall of Lesnar's rookie year, though, proved absolutely essential to the Next Big Thing's credibility and perception.

Labeled and promoted as the star of the future, Lesnar needed a match in which he was physically tested, bloodied even, and allowed to fight from underneath. He needed it to not come easy and Undertaker, the American Badass, made sure that it did not.

Lesnar was battered and beaten throughout the match but mustered the fury that had become a trademark of his in-ring performance and finished an even more battered, bloodied, and beaten Undertaker with an F-5 to win the the match, retain his title, and pass the biggest test of his young career.

Some may argue that the match is properly rated among other Fall classics, but considering its quality and historical significance, it still is not mentioned enough in the pantheon of either man's best.

5. John Cena vs. Dean Ambrose vs. AJ Styles (No Mercy 2016)

The Triple Threat Match for the WWE Championship inexplicably kicked off No Mercy 2016, the first SmackDown-exclusive pay-per-view event following the brand split, as AJ Styles defended his title against Dean Ambrose and John Cena.

A high-energy, red-hot start to the show, it saw the three top dogs on the blue brand deliver a match full of creative and unique counters and spots that concluded with the vile champion resorting to underhanded tactics to emerge victoriously.

In the match's closing seconds, The Phenomenal One entered the ring with a weapon, blasted Cena with it, and pinned him. It was a finish that combated the never-before-seen originality of the sequences, reversals, and false finishes with one blatant and unabashed swing of a chair.

After the audience had been taken on this dramatic and unpredictable ride, the most creative of all moments was the cheap one utilized by the Face That Runs The Place that earned him the tainted victory.

4. The Rock vs. Chris Jericho (No Mercy 2001)

It was the question hanging over his WCW Championship match-up against The Rock at No Mercy in 2001.

For over 23 minutes, Y2J proved he could hang with The Great One, kicking out of the iconic Superstar's best stuff and leaving him reeling with his own signature offense. No matter what he could do, though, he could not keep the competitor down for the count.

That is, until The Alliance's Stephanie McMahon appeared with a steel chair, only to be turned away. With the official distracted by the ECW owner's presence at ringside, Jericho dropped Rock with a Breakdown and won the title that eluded him to that point in his career.

It was a watershed moment and one that ushered in Jericho's first main event run, just as the WCW/ECW Invasion storyline neared its end.

3. The Hardy Boyz vs. Edge and Christian (No Mercy 1999)

Who knows what the landscape of professional wrestling would look like if The Hardy Boyz, Edge, and Christian never clashed in the Tag Team Ladder Match that concluded the Terri Invitational Tournament.

That match provided an alternative to the hardcore brawls of the Attitude Era and opened the door for young, athletic, creative Superstars to showcase their talents on a grand stage.

The fans in Cleveland were ready to embrace the new, exciting, fresh faces, greeting their physical sacrifice with thunderous reactions and a standing ovation for both teams after Jeff Hardy retrieved the $100,000 hanging from the ceiling.

A revolutionary match-up that was quickly overshadowed by the Triple Threat Ladder Match months later at WrestleMania 2000 and the first and second TLC matches, its importance to the landscape of professional wrestling and the introduction of new styles is probably not taken into enough consideration.

A legitimate classic, regardless of what season it took place in.

2. Shawn Michaels vs. Chris Jericho (No Mercy 2008)

The best rivalry of 2008 was Shawn Michaels vs. Chris Jericho, bar none.

Channeling a sicker, more deranged and despicable side of himself than fans had ever seen before, Jericho brutally assaulted his childhood hero to instigate a heel turn. From there, he put him on the shelf, then accidentally punched his wife.

He even captured the World Heavyweight Championship at Unforgiven in September, wrapping up a night in which he had been physically pummeled by HBK with a toothless grin and 20 pounds of gold.

With months of build, Michaels and Jericho took to the squared circle for the concluding match in their rivalry. With the World Heavyweight Championship hung overhead, they competed in a match they had both previously had success in: a Ladder Match.

Opting for physicality and brutality over awe-inspiring spots popularized by the Hardy Boyz, Edge and Christian, and the Dudley Boyz, they delivered an instant classic that had fans cringing for all of the right reasons.

By night's end, Jericho overcame a vengeful Michaels, retained his title, and put a near flawless cap on the epic program.

1. Shawn Michaels vs. Mankind (In Your House: Mind Games)

Shawn Michaels' defense of the WWE Championship against Mankind at the In Your House: Mind Games pay-per-view is, arguably, the best match in company history that not nearly enough people talk about.

Not only was it essential to establishing Mankind as a main event attraction, but it was key to Michaels winning further favor with the die-hard members of the WWE fan base that had not previously believed in him as world champion.

The sadistic, masked villain pulled out of Michaels an edginess and toughness that had been lacking from the Heartbreak Kid's presentation. The company's lead babyface relentlessly attacked Mankind, threw caution to the wind, and was as aggressive as ever while doing so.

The match was mutually beneficial, left the bloodthirsty fans in Philadelphia hanging on every big spot, and featured a logical conclusion that saw The Undertaker pop out of a casket meant for HBK and lay into Mankind, advancing their legendary rivalry in a way that made sense.

Though it did not have a definitive finish, it did not need one and that, perhaps, is the greatest compliment that can be paid to it and its participants.

Three decades after it closed out the September 1996 show, it is still one of the best main events the company has ever produced, albeit one that is not mentioned nearly enough compared to others from the competitors' lengthy resumes.

Unlike drafted prospects who enter an organization with a history of selection, Bowman had to earn his way after going undrafted. articles.title: How Iran’s rowers kept training through war and bombing raids to win first-ever Asian Games gold in historic six-medal haul
articles.summary: Iran's rowing team achieved a historic milestone at the Asian Games, winning their first-ever gold medals in women's rowing amidst challenging circumstances due to conflict. This article highlights their remarkable journey and accomplishments.
articles.body: Iran's rowers arrived at the Asian Games after a preparation unlike anything they had experienced before, with their training camp cancelled and athletes scattered across cities as the war disrupted life across the country. Yet when they finally returned to the water in Nagoya, they produced one of the strongest days in the history of Iranian women's rowing, winning gold medals, adding silver and bronze, and turning months of uncertainty into a remarkable haul.Iran's rowers delivered a historic day in NagoyaThe breakthrough began with Fatemeh Mojallal, who won the women's lightweight single sculls in 7:24.57 to claim the first Asian Games gold medal for Iranian women's rowing.Later, Kimia Zarei and Zeinab Norouzi added another gold in the women's lightweight double sculls, winning in 6:53.93 and finishing 5.31 seconds ahead of Hong Kong, with Japan taking bronze.Iran's medal haul continued in the women's quadruple sculls, where Mahsa Javer, Soha Fakhri, Saghi Maleki and Hengameh Kamyab finished second in 6:27.24, behind China and ahead of Japan.Zarei and Norouzi also collected a silver medal in the women's double sculls, finishing behind the Chinese pair with a time of 6:55.78, while Amir Hossein Mahmoudpour won silver in the lightweight men's single sculls.Mojallal also added a bronze medal in the single sculls, making the Nagaragawa International Regatta Course the setting for a particularly productive day for Iran’s rowing team. The venue features a straight 2,000-meter course and previously hosted the 2005 World Rowing Championships, the first World Rowing Championships held in Asia.The six-medal haul was built around the country's first women's rowing golds at the Asian Games, with Mojallal and the Zarei-Norouzi partnership reaching the top of the podium on the same day.For Zarei and Norouzi, the achievement also continued a partnership that had already produced international success before Nagoya. The pair won gold at the 2025 Asian Rowing Championships in Vietnam, finishing first in the final in 7:30.22 against crews from India, Vietnam, Thailand and Hong Kong. They had also won multiple gold medals at the 2024 Asian Rowing Championships in Samarkand.Their success in Nagoya therefore represented the latest step in an established partnership, although the circumstances surrounding their preparation this time were dramatically different.Their training camp was cancelled when the war beganThe Israel-Iran conflict had disrupted Iran’s sporting preparations months before the Asian Games, with the federation cancelling its training camp and sending the rowers back to their respective homes.Zarei returned to Hamadan, while her teammates went back to their own cities. With the athletes separated and unable to train together on the water, the federation provided each rower with an ergometer so they could maintain their fitness at home.For roughly 45 days, Zarei trained alone, following a programme sent by her coach and covering about 20 kilometres a day on the indoor rowing machine.“I was preparing to start training, and then I heard the bombing sounds,” Zarei said in a conversation with The Indian Express. “It was so close to our home. When you looked out of the window, you could see the smoke.The disruption was not simply a matter of finding somewhere else to exercise. When the bombing intensified, athletes sometimes had to leave their homes or move to other locations, while the training schedule continued whenever circumstances allowed.“All the cities in Iran were affected by the war,” Zarei said. “In the first month of the war, it was really hard, harder than before.”The federation's decision to provide ergometers gave the athletes a way to continue preparing despite the collapse of their normal training environment.“We faced a lot of difficulties after the war began, but we wanted to show that we are strong. We have given every rower an ergometer so they could continue training at home,” federation chief Mohsen Shadi Naghadeh told The Indian Express.For Zarei, training and simply staying safe became intertwined during those first weeks.“It was both of them,” she said when asked whether she was trying to save her life or trying to row.Speaking to OCA News, Zarei described the decision to return to training despite the continuing conflict and the significance she attached to what they were trying to achieve.“Every day, I did 20 kilometres on the erg then we got back into camp even though there was still a war in our country,” she said. “It was a big risk for us but we risked our lives because we wanted this moment and we wanted this medal for Iranian girls and athletes, Asian Games medals really matter.”The Iranian women's kabaddi team faced similar disruption, with its training camp also affected by the conflict before the players moved between cities and eventually travelled to Sonepat in India in August, where they trained twice a day and played practice matches to rebuild their rhythm.The rowers eventually returned to camp and resumed training on the water at Urmia, where the federation had access to a two-kilometre course, but the weeks spent indoors remained an important part of what they had endured to reach Nagoya.Zarei had spent three years trying to erase one fourth-place finishThe 2026 Asian Games also gave Zarei a chance to settle something that had stayed with her since the previous edition.At the Hangzhou Asian Games, she finished fourth and missed out on a medal by only a quarter of a second, becoming the only member of Iran's rowing team to leave without a medal. Norouzi, by contrast, had won two silver medals at those Games.“It was really a hard moment,” Zarei said.The disappointment changed her approach during the three years that followed. Inspired by her mother, who taught her to be independent, work hard and not rely on others, Zarei changed aspects of her training and diet and began using social media to promote the positive side of being an elite female athlete.“It can be positive in a way that you try to motivate the girls at home, try to show them and try to share your experiences with them,” she said.“Especially in the country where I live, because in Iran we have very unique challenges in my country, especially this year.”The partnership with Norouzi also continued to develop, culminating in their gold at the 2025 Asian Rowing Championships in Vietnam and building on the multiple gold medals won at the 2024 edition in Samarkand.By the time they reached the Asian Games final in Nagoya, Zarei and Mojallal had already spent years competing at the highest level and building towards this moment. Their preparations had been repeatedly interrupted, and the disruption caused by the conflict had made consistent training difficult. Still, they arrived in Nagoya with years of work behind them and finished the job with gold.Zarei captured what the medal meant to her after the race.“Three years of hard work, being motivated, trying to stay positive, trying to believe in myself and believing in God,” she said. “Today, I’ve got first place.”The gold was for Iranian girls and athletesWhen Zarei and Norouzi crossed the finish line first in Nagoya, Zarei splashed the water and broke down in tears. The medal came after the disappointment of Hangzhou, years of preparation and weeks of training alone during the conflict.Throughout that period, she said, her focus stayed on the medal, her family and the people she wanted to represent.“The only thing was thinking about the medal, thinking about my people, thinking about my family and my future,” Zarei said. “Because this medal really matters for Iranian people, especially Iranian girls.”“I cried,” she added. “It was a moment that I really cannot explain in words.”For Norouzi, the gold was the result of a demanding preparation that required them to push through difficult circumstances.“I have a very good feeling and it cannot be described,” she said. “We went through very hard training to win this medal and endured a lot of hardship to achieve this valuable medal.”She dedicated the victory to the Iranian public.“I dedicate this medal to the dear people of Iran, who have always supported the athletes and whose prayers accompany the Iranian national team members,” Norouzi said. “We always fight for the people of Iran, and this gold medal is for the dear people of Iran.”The road to the Nagoya medals was far from straightforward, with athletes separated from their teammates, confined to their homes for extended periods and forced to replace water training with indoor ergometer sessions.The Iranian rowing team had spent months preparing under difficult circumstances, with training disrupted by the conflict and athletes separated from their teammates. Zarei spent 45 days rowing alone in her room, sometimes with explosions close enough for smoke to be visible from her window, while the rest of the team continued preparing in similarly harsh conditions.In Nagoya, the team delivered a stellar performance, winning six medals, including Iran’s first-ever rowing gold medal at the Asian Games.Stay updated with the latest Asian Games 2026 news, check the Asian Games medal tally and complete Asian Games schedule.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: ‘Unstoppable’ Rumesh revives Sri Lanka’s glory, one javelin throw at a time
articles.summary: A gold at the Asian Games will cap off an unprecedented season for the world number one.
articles.body:
In a small coastal town just south of the Sri Lankan capital, Colombo, a young Rumesh Pathirage daydreamed about running away from school to a field where he could practise fast bowling, running, or anything other than being buried in books.

Academic excellence was not the promised path to glory for him. No, his path was on a synthetic rubber track, from which he would launch his javelin until it landed in the history books and made him world number one. Pathirage was destined to carry Sri Lanka to the upper echelons of sporting glory.

Losing is not in Pathirage’s vocabulary for 2026. Since February, he has won all but one of the competitions he has contested. He is the only thrower this year and the fourth in history to breach the 92-metre mark twice in a season — rare in the javelin books — and the only Sri Lankan to win the prestigious Diamond League final, the island nation’s first Commonwealth gold medallist in 20 years and the only South Asian to win a medal at the inaugural Ultimate Championships this month.

Come Saturday, the 23-year-old from Kalutara will attempt to win his final title of the season — the Asian Games gold — and attempt to break the 92.97m Asian record en route to continental triumph.

“The biggest prize is winning Olympic gold for Sri Lanka,” a nonchalant Pathirage told Al Jazeera in an online interview after the Zurich Diamond League victory, which saw him cross the 92m mark for a record second time. Given his track record, the 6-foot-1-inch (185.4cm) phenom could very well make that happen too.

An Olympic gold would be a first for Sri Lanka, as many of Pathirage’s accolades have been. But an Olympic podium finish was first achieved by Susanthika Jayasinghe, Sri Lanka’s track star who won bronze in the women’s 200m sprint at Sydney 2000, before it was upgraded to silver due to a doping disqualification.

Like Pathirage, Jayasinghe found international success in the junior circuit before bagging major wins in the big league. Her legacy, however, was bittersweet, marred by political interference, alleged tampered drug tests and sexual violence by federal sports officials, and next to no support from Sri Lanka’s athletics federation. But it paved the way for young athletes like Pathirage to dream of a future as track and field’s biggest stars.

Pathirage is already paying his success forward. When well-wishers offered financial assistance to replace his javelins broken days before the Asian Games , he requested that the money be redirected to struggling athletes instead. After all, he was in their shoes not too long ago.

His main source of support has been the Sri Lankan air force, which Pathirage represents as an athlete, and a generous diaspora have helped fund his training, equipment and extensive international travel for competitions.

That no major international sportswear brand has signed Pathirage, despite him being world number one, speaks volumes about the European chokehold that overshadows success from South Asian athletes like Pathirage and Pakistani javelin thrower Arshad Nadeem.

“If you take athletes of my level, I’m the only one who doesn’t have international brand sponsorship,” Pathirage rued of the “sorry situation”, although he understands that Sri Lanka is a small market for sportswear giants. In comparison, European athletes who are nowhere near the top even in their region have sponsorship deals with brands like Adidas, Puma and Nike.

That the Sri Lankan diaspora has repeatedly stepped up to support Pathirage en route to sporting greatness reflects just how much his triumphs at this level mean to them.

They have followed him across the Diamond League circuit, cheering and waving the Sri Lankan flag, stepped in spontaneously to translate English to Sinhalese for media interviews, and waited patiently for an autograph after he’s bagged yet another gold medal.

Many were Pathirage’s age when they fled Sri Lanka during the devastating 1983-2009 civil war. For them, he is the future of a nation they never experienced, his translator Ranil Jayaneththi told Al Jazeera from Zurich, Switzerland, where the Sri Lankan businessman is now based.

“He’s the most exciting thing to happen to us since Susanthika,” said Jayaneththi, whose smile seemed permanent from the night before when he saw the javelin star in all his glory.

“To go through the history that Sri Lanka went through,” he paused before continuing, “it was sports that gave people hope.”

Meanwhile, his family has always been his pillar of strength, safety net and loudest cheerleaders.

“I wouldn’t be where I am without them,” Pathirage said of his parents and two siblings. “Right from when they let me pursue athletics full-time instead of academics till my early career, I owe them everything.”

Athletics is somewhat of a family thing; Pathirage occasionally mentors his younger brother in javelin, which he switched to after excelling in discus throw, the event their father contested decades ago.

Sri Lanka is not a sporting powerhouse, nor does it boast exceptional facilities, but it gave the likes of Pathirage and Jayasinghe a grassroots platform to springboard to global stardom.

Across the country, school- and regional-level competitions prepare younger athletes for the national stage under the guidance of local coaches, some of whom receive international training. Coaching and sports management are also offered at several Sri Lankan universities now.

Under the tutelage of Tony Prasanna, Pathirage’s throws have steadily progressed from the 60m range in 2019 to mid-80m figures more recently that have secured gold at the Asian Throwing Championships. He also competes regularly in Australia, home to a sizeable Sri Lankan population who fled the civil war.

It was there that Pathirage met Ella Wardlaw, an athlete representative who manages his competition schedule, media commitments and sponsorships.

“Rumesh is unstoppable; he’s been hungry for wins all season,” Wardlaw told Al Jazeera from Zurich. The Australian lawyer-turned-manager has seen Pathirage’s rise from an underdog nervously navigating the international stage to dominating it.

“He thrives on pressure, but he’s really in competition with himself a lot of the time.”

When asked whether the goal is consistency with his wins or 90m-plus throws, Pathirage said, “The goal is to improve on what I have achieved … My mindset is to stay a winner. I concentrate on achieving what I can.”

He is indifferent to the media hype that many of his competitors crave. “I’m only doing this interview because my manager said I have to,” he joked. Neither does he care for celebrity status. His humility is apparent in the low-key social media presence he maintains, the demure victory celebrations born of a performance that does all the talking for him.

What he really wants is to be a role model for future athletes in the cricket-crazy nation.

“I want to inspire the younger generation to see my success and know that other pathways await them,” said Pathirage.

articles.summary: The person who convinced Vince McMahon to step down from TKO has now been revealed, and it was someone very close to McMahon.
articles.body: The person who convinced Vince McMahon to step down from TKO has now been revealed, and it was someone very close to McMahon. The situation related to Vince McMahon's departure from WWE and TKO has remained a significant part of the company's corporate history. Identifying the person who reportedly encouraged McMahon to step down provides further insight into the leadership changes that reshaped WWE.According to details discussed in Ari Emanuel's book, Stephanie McMahon was the person who convinced Vince McMahon to step down from TKO in January 2024. Even, WWE insider, Dave Meltzer reportedly explained that Stephanie's involvement had been known privately but had not previously been publicly confirmed. It is important to note that Vince McMahon left TKO Group Holdings on January 26, 2024. He left the role of TKO Executive Chairman and as a member of the TKO Board of Directors.Vince McMahon's daughter, Stephanie McMahon, reportedly convinced her father to resignVince McMahon's daughter, Stephanie McMahon, has reportedly convinced her father to resign from TKO in January 2024. Wrestling journalist Dave Meltzer reportedly explained that Stephanie's involvement had been known privately but had not previously been publicly confirmed.Vince McMahon's resignation came amid the fallout from Janel Grant's lawsuit, which named McMahon, WWE and John Laurinaitis. McMahon denied wrongdoing.This sitaution further escalated and created pressure on TKO leadership, including TKO President and Chief Operating Officer Mark Shapiro. The lawsuit against the former TKO Executive Chairman was originally filed in January 2024. It accused McMahon of sexual assault, sex trafficking, and coercion during Grant's time as a WWE employee.McMahon has repeatedly denied the allegations, while WWE has also denied wrongdoing. The federal case was later officially closed in July 2026 after the parties agreed to dismiss the action with prejudice while preserving claims and defenses for private arbitration.Reports suggest that TKO's corporate structure meant that McMahon could not simply be fired, making the resignation look like the only way he could leave his position. The company had to navigate the situation while dealing with growing scrutiny surrounding the allegations and sponsor concerns.McMahon ultimately resigned as TKO's Executive Chairman on January 26, 2024, after Stephanie McMahon convinced him to step down, and left the company's board. His departure marked a major change in the corporate leadership of WWE, a company he had controlled for decades.Vince McMahon spent decades being the person who was impossible to remove from WWE, but this time the final conversation apparently came from inside his own family. articles.title: Before Anthony Joshua vs Tyson Fury’s decade-long wait, Mike Tyson and Evander Holyfield took 12 years to finally fight
articles.summary: The wait for Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua has become one of boxing’s longest-running heavyweight stories.
articles.body: The wait for Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua has become one of boxing’s longest-running heavyweight stories. The British rivals have talked about fighting for years, but the much-anticipated clash has repeatedly remained out of reach.But heavyweight boxing has seen even longer waits. Mike Tyson and Evander Holyfield first appeared destined to meet in the late 1980s. Contracts were signed, plans were made, and then everything fell apart. It took years before they finally shared a ring, creating one of boxing’s most famous rivalries.Mike Tyson and Evander Holyfield showed how long a heavyweight fight can takeThe Mike Tyson-Evander Holyfield story began long before their professional rivalry. The two heavyweights had crossed paths at the 1984 American Olympic boxing trials. A pool-table incident added another layer to their relationship, and their careers continued moving toward an inevitable showdown.By October 1989, that fight appeared to be finally happening. Contracts for Tyson and Holyfield had reportedly been signed for a summer 1990 meeting.The planned fight was scheduled for June 18, 1990, in Atlantic City. Then came one of boxing’s biggest shocks. On February 11, 1990, Tyson lost his heavyweight titles to Buster Douglas in Tokyo.A new agreement was eventually reached on July 11, 1991, at a New York hotel. The fight was set for November 8, 1991, at Caesars Palace in Las Vegas.The financial numbers showed just how important the fight had become. The fighters were expected to split a $45 million guarantee, with Holyfield receiving $30 million. The event was projected to generate around $100 million.Once again, however, the fight collapsed.Tyson was arrested in July 1991 after travelling to Indiana for a beauty pageant. He was charged with rape. The proposed fight was pushed back, with January 1992 discussed as a possible new date. Then Tyson suffered a rib injury. The fight was off again.Tyson was later convicted and sent to prison. For several years, a Tyson-Holyfield fight looked impossible.But boxing rarely closes the door completely on a major money fight.After Tyson was released from prison in 1995, discussions about Holyfield resumed. The matchup still had enormous commercial value.Tyson regained the heavyweight championship in 1996. Holyfield, meanwhile, had experienced his own difficult road. He had lost the title, regained it and then lost it again.Finally, the fight was officially announced for November 1996 at the MGM Grand in Las Vegas.Many expected Tyson to win. Instead, Holyfield delivered one of the biggest upsets of his career. He stopped Tyson in the 11th round.The rematch in 1997 became even more infamous. Tyson was disqualified after biting Holyfield’s ears in what became known as the “Bite of the Century.”That history provides an interesting backdrop to Fury and Joshua. Joshua first called for the fight in April 2016, after winning a heavyweight world title. More than a decade has now passed since the rivalry first became a serious talking point.The circumstances are different, but the pattern is familiar. For the first time in his career, AEW star MJF is atop Pro Wrestling Illustrated magazine's prestigious PWI 500 list.

MJF was chosen as the No. 1 wrestler of the year for the 2026 PWI 500, beating out WWE's Cody Rhodes, who topped the list in both 2024 and 2025.

Ahead of the release of the entire 2026 PWI 500 in the latest issue of Pro Wrestling Illustrated , the publication revealed the top 10 on Thursday:

Ranking WWE's 10 Forgotten Classic Matches of 2025 🔢

During the evaluation period for the 2026 PWI 500, which lasted from August 2025 until July 2026, MJF held the AEW World Championship twice.

His previous high water mark in the PWI 500 was a sixth-place finish in 2023, but the charismatic heel can now be recognized as the standard bearer in pro wrestling.

MJF is the third AEW wrestler to top the PWI 500 since the inception of the company, joining Jon Moxley in 2020 and Kenny Omega in 2021.

Had Rhodes beaten out MJF, he would have become the first wrestler in history to be named No. 1 in the PWI 500 in three consecutive years.

Another major takeaway from the 2026 PWI 500 is the emergence of rising stars in WWE, as both Trick Williams and Oba Femi made their debuts in the top 10.

articles.title: Chess Olympiad Round 8: India miss chance to close in as Gukesh draws; Savitha Shri saves women’s day
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: India had a smooth sail in the open section of the 2026 Chess Olympiad until their Round 6 game against hosts Uzbekistan in Samarkand.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: India had a smooth sail in the open section of the 2026 Chess Olympiad until their Round 6 game against hosts Uzbekistan in Samarkand. We all know what happened there.With the other three boards drawn, Nihal Sarin had an advantage against Nodirbek Yakubboev, only to blunder his queen, the match slipped from India's grip, handing Uzbekistan the lead in the title race. While Sarin's blunder dominated the post-match discussion in chess circles, some also asked whether world champion Dommaraju Gukesh could have pushed his own game a little further instead of settling for a draw.Vidit Gujrathi, briefly joining ChessBase India's commentary panel on his rest day, brushed the suggestion aside. "Gukesh plays his own game," he said. "If he feels there is a chance, he pushes till the very end." India needed exactly that in the Round 8 match-up against Azerbaijan's Mahammad Muradli.With the other three boards ending in draws, Gukesh needed a win to settle the match and keep India's title defence alive, a defence that had looked bleak even a day earlier.As Germany beat Uzbekistan at the other end of the hall on Thursday, a win for Gukesh would have put India within touching distance of the new leaders. He pushed for one, right until the position simplified into a draw he couldn't avoid.Playing white in a Najdorf Sicilian, Gukesh went for the ambitious 7.Qf3, and Muradli responded accurately with 7...h6 and some active queen manoeuvres. Both sides simplified quickly in the early middlegame, with 16.Bxc4 Qxc4 17.Qd3 Qxd3 leading into a queenless position. Gukesh carved out some queenside space with 27.b4 and 28.b5, while Muradli locked down the centre and activated his king in response.The game turned into a fierce time-pressure battle from there.By move 35, both players had under two minutes each, but Gukesh kept the position balanced. Even after the time control, the resulting rook-and-bishop ending proved impossible to crack — Muradli's active rook checks, starting with 48...Rb2+, forced Gukesh's king into a repeating sequence, and neither side could make further progress.The players shook hands on a draw after 56...Rb2+, a resilient defensive display from Muradli against sustained pressure from the world champion.As things stand, Uzbekistan and Germany lead the standings with 14 points apiece. A chasing pack on 13 includes China, Azerbaijan, the United States, India, Armenia and France, with all hoping for further slip-ups at the top that they can pounce on.Savitha Shri saves Indian women's day againSavitha Shri's dominant run on Board 4 continued into Thursday, stretching her winning streak to seven as India's women held Kazakhstan to a 2-2 draw. It was Savitha, once again, who came to her side's rescue after the team fell behind when Alua Nurman beat Vaishali Rameshbabu on Board 2.With Divya Deshmukh and Koneru Humpy having already drawn their games against Meruert Kamalidenova and Bibisara Assaubayeva, respectively, India needed a win on Board 4 to stay in the title hunt, and Savitha delivered.It was a hard-fought battle against Elnaz Kaliakhmet, played out through an Italian Game (Giuoco Piano) that turned into a long strategic grind. After the quiet opening moves, 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 d6, both sides manoeuvred patiently before the middlegame tension picked up.Savitha's unusual 11.Ra4 and the rook manoeuvres that followed showed a willingness to play the long game, and the position tipped in her favour after 25.Nf5 gave White a more comfortable structure. Queens came off soon after, leading into a demanding rook-and-pawn endgame.With both players deep into time trouble, Savitha's technique held up under pressure. Moves like 52.Rd5+ and 54.dxe4 kept her ahead practically, while 59.Rxd3 simplified the position into a winning king-and-rook ending. Kaliakhmet resigned after 62.Ra2.India remain in the chasing pack in the women's section too, with China leading on 15 points, Kazakhstan and Mongolia on 14, and India on 13. With three rounds still to go, the race for both titles is far from settled. articles.title: Panthers CB Mike Jackson may have the best take on LB Devin Lloyd's insane Week 2 performance
articles.summary: Panthers CB Mike Jackson on LB Devin Lloyd's Week 2 performance: "You can't do that on a video game."
articles.body:
Statistically speaking, the Carolina Panthers defense is not off to a great start this season. After giving up 59 points to the Chicago Bears in Week 1, their numbers are still a bit lopsided—even though they almost shut out the Atlanta Falcons in a dominant Week 2 win .

Heading into Week 3, the Panthers rank last in rushing yards allowed (224) and they're tied with the Miami Dolphins for the third-worst scoring defense in the league (31.0 points per game).

This is why context is so important—because Carolina's defense is looking better than it has in years, especially at the linebacker position.

That's where both Devin Lloyd and Bobby Okereke stood out on Sunday, with the former putting in one of the best games in franchise history at the position. That's really something considering the number of elite linebackers who have passed through over the last 30 years—including Hall of Famers Sam Mills and Luke Kuechly and team greats Dan Morgan and Thomas Davis .

Lloyd's output— the first ever that has yielded nine tackles, a sack, two interceptions and an interception return for a touchdown—has drawn some high praise.

Head coach Dave Canales said it was maybe the best game he's ever seen from a linebacker in 17 years in the NFL. It was certainly the best of the conference, as the league named him the NFC Defensive Player of the Week .

But the coolest take may belong to cornerback Mike Jackson .

"I ain't never seen a game like that by any defensive player ever," Jackson told reporters on Wednesday. "You can't do that on a video game."

To be sure, it takes a real sicko to user-control an off-ball linebacker in Madden—but it is definitely possible.

That doesn't take anything away anything from Lloyd's performance, which raises the ceiling for what this unit can accomplish—both in 2026 and as long as he's wearing a Panthers uniform.

articles.title: Father of Penguins forward Andrei Kuzmenko dies in bear mauling in Russia

articles.body:
The father of Pittsburgh Penguins forward Andrei Kuzmenko has died in a bear attack in Russia.

Ren TV reported that Alexander Kuzmenko, a hockey coach, was mauled Sept. 23 in the Tuva region. A bear reportedly came out of the woods quickly and bit Kuzmenko. His companions were able to free him from the animal, but attempts to treat him failed.

"The Pittsburgh Penguins organization was deeply saddened, this morning, to learn of the passing of Andrei Kuzmenko's father, Alexander," Penguins GM Kyle Dubas said in a statement Thursday. "Our deepest thoughts and sympathies are with the Kuzmenko family and their loved ones as they grieve the loss of Alexander. We ask that the privacy of Andrei and the Kuzmenko family be respected at this time.

"Andrei chose to be surrounded by his teammates and practice with the team this morning before returning to Moscow to be with his family this afternoon. Andrei and the Kuzmenko family have the full support of the Penguins organization during this time."

Bear attacks in this area of the country have surged in 2026. According to Ren TV, 15 people have been attacked across four provinces, with experts blaming a poor harvest of berries and pine nuts.

Andrei Kuzmenko signed a one-year deal with the Penguins on July 1 and had just reported to Pittsburgh for training camp. The 30-year-old has 85 goals and 97 assists across four NHL seasons with the Vancouver Canucks , Calgary Flames , Los Angeles Kings and Philadelphia Flyers .

articles.title: Somerset title hopes fade as Lawrence stars for Surrey
articles.summary: Dan Lawrence hits his sixth County Championship century of the season as Surrey dominate the opening day of the final Division One match with Somerset.
articles.body:
Rothesay County Championship, Division One, Cooper Associates County Ground, Taunton (day one)

Surrey 327-4: Lawrence 105*, Sibley 72, Foakes 64*; Gregory 1-56

Dan Lawrence hit his sixth County Championship century of the season as Surrey dominated the opening day of the final Division One match with Somerset at the Cooper Associates Ground, Taunton.

The visitors ran up 327-4 after winning the toss, Lawrence top-scoring with an unbeaten 105 off 136 balls, with nine fours and four sixes. The innings maintained his record of going on to three figures every time he has made fifty in red ball cricket this summer.

Dom Sibley contributed 72 off 188 deliveries and Ben Foakes 64 not out as Somerset saw their flickering hopes of a first ever Championship title all but snuffed out in front of nearly 3,000 expectant supporters.

The match began in bright sunshine and it soon looked a good toss to win as the pitch offered scant assistance to the Somerset seamers. In the hope of boosting their hopes of maximum batting points to keep title hopes alive, the hosts brought the boundary ropes in on both sides of the wicket.

Soon it was Surrey capitalising on the favourable batting conditions. As early as the eighth over, Somerset skipper Lewis Gregory turned to spin, introducing Jack Leach from the River End.

Rory Burns had no intention of letting the experienced left-armer settle into a line and length, slog-sweeping him for six in only his second over. And when Craig Overton began his second spell, switched to the Marcus Trescothick Pavilion End, Burns cleared the ropes again with a pull shot.

The Surrey opener looked in prime form. But, having reached 31 off 44 balls, he misjudged a sweep off Leach and top-edged a catch to Tom Abell at short fine-leg. The stand with Sibley had put 47 on the board with few alarms.

Ryan Patel contributed 16 in helping advance the total to 78 when caught at slip pushing forward defensively to off-spinner Archie Vaughan. But Sibley batted comfortably through the morning session to be unbeaten on 35 at lunch, which was taken at 86-2.

Ollie Pope began the afternoon session by lofting Vaughan over long-on for six and, like Burns, looked ready to be positive at every opportunity, while Sibley played the anchor role, reaching a typically solid half-century off 138 balls, with eight fours.

A Sibley boundary to fine leg brought up a fifty stand and it came as a surprise when, with the total on 131, Pope fell leg before on the back foot, playing across a straight ball from Gregory, wicketkeeper James Rew having just moved to stand up to the stumps.

On 59, Sibley survived a confident lbw shout from Leach, but soon another useful partnership developed as Lawrence played with characteristic aggression, smacking Leach over wide long-on for six.

With tea approaching, Sibley was lured into a trap, glancing a ball directed at leg stump by Migael Pretorius, who had been awarded his Somerset county cap before play commenced, straight to the perfectly positioned Abell at leg-slip. It was 174-4 and nine more runs were added before the interval.

Lawrence had glided to 34 and the final session saw him produce arguably the shot of the day with a glorious straight-driven four off Pretorius. His sixth boundary, a flowing off-drive off Vaughan, took him to an 86-ball half-century.

Foakes was looking equally at ease as the pair brought up a century stand off 156 balls. He moved fluently to the third fifty of the innings off 93 balls as the scoring rate accelerated, Lawrence slog-sweeping Leach for a big six over mid-wicket and then a straighter one in the same over.

It was looking all too easy for Surrey as stumps approached, Lawrence going to a typically easy-on-the-eye hundred with his fourth six, smashed over wide long-on off Leach in the final over. The unbroken stand with Foakes was worth 153.

articles.title: Zay Flowers Injury Update: Ravens WR’s Hamstring Issue Puts Sunday Status in Doubt
articles.summary: The Baltimore Ravens are heading into their Week 3 matchup against the Dallas Cowboys already short on some important pieces in the passing game. Zay Flowers...
articles.body:
The Baltimore Ravens are heading into their Week 3 matchup against the Dallas Cowboys already short on some important pieces in the passing game. Zay Flowers has been the biggest name to watch after missing Week 2 with a hamstring issue, and the Ravens have spent this week monitoring whether its top receiver can make it back in time for Sunday.

The Ravens have reason to be cautious with Flowers, especially after the same hamstring problem already forced him out of the second half of Week 1 and kept him sidelined against the New Orleans Saints .

Ian Rapoport Raises Concern Over Zay Flowers ' Week 3 Status

NFL insider Ian Rapoport reported on September 24 that the Ravens are taking a careful approach with Flowers because they want the wide receiver available throughout the season. However, his latest practice status has created another hurdle ahead of Sunday's matchup with the Cowboys.

"Did not practice yesterday, that does not bode well for his participation on Sunday."

That update matters because Flowers has already missed one full game with the injury. He aggravated the hamstring during the Ravens' Week 1 win over the Indianapolis Colts after putting together a huge first half, catching five passes for 150 yards and a touchdown.

He then sat out the Ravens' Week 2 loss to the Saints. Now, with the receiver missing Wednesday's practice ahead of the Cowboys game, the possibility of another absence is becoming harder to ignore. There had still been some optimism earlier in the week. The Ravens head coach, Jesse Minter, described Flowers as day-to-day and said the team would consider what was best for the receiver before deciding his status; however, Rapoport's Thursday update provides a more cautious outlook.

The timing is especially important for the Ravens because the receiver room is already dealing with another setback. Ja'Kobi Lane is on injured reserve, leaving Rashod Bateman , Devontez Walker , LaJohntay Wester , Elijah Sarratt, and Chris Moore among the available wideouts.

Bateman would likely take on an even larger role if Flowers cannot return. He already stepped into the spotlight during Week 2, giving the QB Lamar Jackson another reliable option while Flowers watched from the sideline.

Yet, the 26-year-old's absence would remove the Ravens' most explosive receiving threat. His five-catch, 150-yard performance against the Colts showed how quickly he can change a game when healthy.

For now, Flowers has not officially been ruled out ; however, with the Ravens being careful about his hamstring and Rapoport noting that Wednesday's absence "does not bode well" for Sunday, his status remains one of the biggest injury questions heading into Baltimore's Week 3 clash with Dallas.

articles.title: Matthew Golden Fantasy Week 3 Start or Sit: Close to a Flex, Not Quite There
articles.summary: Golden is WR43 in PFN’s Week 3 rankings after a dozen targets in the opener and six more against the Jets, plus a 23-yard pass interference he drew that show...
articles.body:
Golden is WR43 in PFN's Week 3 rankings after a dozen targets in the opener and six more against the Jets, plus a 23-yard pass interference he drew that shows up in nobody's box score. The one thing keeping him out of my top 35 is how closely his game mirrors Christian Watson's. If you play him Thursday, use a WR slot rather than the flex.

Should You Start or Sit Matthew Golden in Week 3?

Golden earned a dozen targets in the opener and another six last week against the Jets. Those looks in the overtime win don't include a 23-yard DPI that he forced with Green Bay backed up in the third quarter, a play that nets us nothing as fantasy managers but is good to see.

I'm not there yet with him as a flex option, but I'm not far. We know Jordan Love wants to stretch the field vertically, and given where this run game currently sits, high PROE schemes seem more likely than not until the Josh Jacobs situation gets ironed out.

The last hurdle I have to clear before getting Golden inside of my top-35 at the position is the skill mirroring with Christian Watson. Like his counterpart, speed is a primary weapon for Golden. That can be a net positive with time, but it also creates a low floor in weeks where Watson is winning in a big way.

Against the Falcons, I'm not too worried about a lack of opportunities. If you want to roll the dice on Golden as a flex Thursday night, make sure you're slotting him in a "WR" slot to give yourself flexibility later in the week should an injury pop up on your roster.

articles.title: PWHL announces unique format for first All-Star event in Toronto
articles.summary: The PWHL is bringing its first All-Star tournament to Toronto, Canada, featuring a 3-on-3 format at Scotiabank Arena on March 7, 2027.
articles.body:
The first PWHL All-Star tournament is headed to Toronto, the league announced on Thursday, Sept. 24 , featuring a four-team, 3-on-3 tournament at Scotiabank Arena.

The PWHL-hosted All-Star event will take place March 7, 2027, and will feature a round-robin format between PWHL Canada, PWHL International, PWHL USA, and PWHL Rookies.

The format of the inaugural event follows a similar path as the Winter Olympics in Milan, Italy, where the U.S. women's hockey team beat Canada in 2026.

The starts will be determined by a combination of voting from fans, players and media, while league officials will select reserve players.

The first ranked team will advance directly to the finals while the second and third ranked teams will meet in a semifinal game.

Each team is made up of six forwards, three defenders and one goaltender.

Full programming and event details, including voting, roster construction, ticketing, and gameplay rules, will be announced leading up to the event, league officials say.

The league makes its return to Canada since it first dropped the puck on Jan. 1, 2024, when Toronto hosted New York in the first game in PWHL history at Mattamy Athletic Centre.

The PWHL will start its preseason on Tuesday, Nov. 22.

Detroit will play its first game at 1:30 p.m. on Nov. 23 at the Morgan Firestone Arena in Ancaster, Ottawa, Canada, against the Charge.

articles.title: Shane Steichen: I have confidence in DC Lou Anarumo, no doubt about it
articles.summary: The Colts have gotten off to a poor start on defense in 2026.
articles.body:
The Colts have gotten off to a poor start on defense in 2026.

While the viral social media post claiming that the Colts have allowed the most yards through two games in league history is false, Indianapolis has not been much better than that.

The 2016 Raiders gave up 1,035 total yards in their first two games — ironically going 1-1 in that span.

The 2026, 0-2 Colts have surrendered 1,029 yards and 74 points, both of which rank dead last in the league after losses to the Ravens and Chiefs. Indianapolis has also surrendered a league-worst 7.2 yards per play.

Indianapolis brought in Lou Anarumo as defensive coordinator last year with the expectation that he'd raise the level of play from former coordinator Gus Bradley. But the unit was only marginally improved last year — going from No. 24 in points allowed and No. 29 in yards allowed in 2024 to No. 21 in points allowed and No. 23 in yards allowed in 2025.

Given the historically bad start, head coach Shane Steichen was asked in his Wednesday press conference if he has confidence in Anarumo to be able to turn the unit around.

"Yeah, absolutely. I have confidence in Lou, no doubt about it," Steichen said, via transcript from the team. "He's been doing it for a long time in this league. He's had success in this league, and I have no doubt that this thing will get turned defensively."

Steichen noted the defensive issues begin with poor tackling.

"I think we had a ton of missed tackles last week, last couple weeks, and those are leading to explosive plays, especially in the run game," Steichen said. "And then we've got to be great on the backend in coverage. I mean, it's all part of it. All ties in together. The rush and coverage work together, and we got to get that stuff cleaned up moving forward so we're not giving up those big plays and those yards.

"Again, we want to be better than it was the first two games," Steichen added. "There's no ifs, ands or buts about it. We have to be better there. But I do. I have a lot of confidence in [Anarumo] and what we're doing moving forward. I think there's the communication stuff. We're getting that stuff cleaned up, and again, it goes back to tackling, and fundamentals, and we've got to do a great job of tackling moving forward."

We'll see if the Colts can show improvement when they play the Texans at home on Sunday.

articles.title: ‘Arch has not been that impressive’: Joel Klatt does not hold back on Arch Manning
articles.summary: Texas Longhorns star quarterback Arch Manning is the most high-profile player in college football. But as Fox Sports analyst Joel Klatt points out, that does...
articles.body:
Texas Longhorns star quarterback Arch Manning is the most high-profile player in college football. But as Fox Sports analyst Joel Klatt points out, that doesn't make him the best.

Ahead of a showdown between the top-ranked Texas Longhorns and the unbeaten Tennessee Volunteers in Knoxville, Klatt has made it clear that he's been largely unimpressed by how Manning has performed this year.

While the Longhorns might be undefeated and ranked No. 1 in both the AP Poll and the Coaches Poll, Klatt does not think that Manning has been particularly good individually.

"Now Arch has not lit it on fire this year," Klatt said on his podcast this week . "Listen, that last quarter and a half, if you want to call it that, those last three drives against Ohio State, he was excellent, more gritty than excellent, but he got the job done. Outside of that guys, and I know that this is a contrarian take and no one wants to have it, Arch has not been that impressive.

"I know we all want him to be impressive because of the last name, but he's got to take the next step, and the next step for him is playing well on the road, anticipating throws."

While Manning has obviously been good enough to keep Texas undefeated – which included a gutty comeback win over the then top-ranked Ohio State Buckeyes – Klatt seemingly thinks Manning has more to prove.

"Let's go back to the list I was talking about on Monday when I was talking about Trinidad Chambliss as a quarterback. If you're a great player, you can execute in the passing game, and … your team can rely on the passing game, even if you don't have a run game," Klatt said. "Now, I will say this: I think Texas is a lot better at the line of scrimmage and specifically running the football than they were a year ago. If that shows up for them in this game against Tennessee, then everything's going to be fine, and Arch is going to be out there, and he'll have a good game."

Klatt is not the only one to criticize Manning for the way that he has played this season. After Texas' comeback win over Ohio State, former Alabama national champion quarterback and current college football analyst A.J. McCarron had a harsh assessment of Manning's play, calling the performance "horrible."

"I thought Arch looked horrible, honestly," McCarron said on an appearance on the McCready and Siskey Podcast . "And I love the Manning family. I thought Arch did not look good. If his first read was not open, he looked lost. He hangs on that first progression so long … He stares down his receivers way too much. Look at his last couple of possessions. Just take the fourth quarter. When any big throw, it's to his first progression. He never came off his first progression and hit another big throw … I'm not hating against Arch at all. Like I said, I love the Manning family. Known him since I was young or younger.

"I think Arch has a chance to be good, but I think he's got a lot of growing to do from a pocket awareness standpoint, from a progression standpoint, playing faster. I watched that young kid, the freshman from Tennessee tonight, and I thought him going through progressions looked better than what Arch looks. And Arch has had a whole year of playing experience over him."

Manning has a chance to change the narrative around his play this week.

articles.title: Blackhawks sign Oliver Moore to a 5-year deal worth $4.25 million per year
articles.summary: Oliver Moore had five goals and 14 assists in 51 games for Chicago last season.
articles.body:
CHICAGO — The Chicago Blackhawks signed forward Oliver Moore to a five-year deal, locking up an important piece of their long-term future.

The deal with the 21-year-old Moore carries an average annual value of $4.25 million.

Moore, a first-round pick by Chicago in the 2023 draft, had five goals and 14 assists in 51 games for the Blackhawks last season while averaging just under 13 minutes of ice time per game.

Moore is coming off an offseason in which he made his debut for Team USA at the world championships, picking up three assists.

articles.title: Anthony Gordon opens up on Thomas Tuchel's 'surprise' call during World Cup semi-final
articles.summary: Anthony Gordon has opened up about his 'surprise' at being substituted by Thomas Tuchel shortly after scoring for England in their FIFA World Cup semi-final...
articles.body:
Anthony Gordon has admitted he was "surprised" to be substituted by Thomas Tuchel after giving England the lead in their FIFA World Cup semi-final against Argentina.

Tuchel faced widespread criticism for adopting an overly defensive approach following Gordon's goal against Argentina, though he defended his tactics as England ultimately crumbled and squandered a prime opportunity to reach the final. Gordon became Tuchel's first substitution, replaced by defender Ezri Konsa with over 20 minutes still to play.

When questioned about whether the England boss's decision caught him off guard, Gordon responded via The Mirror : "Yeah, I was, being totally honest. Only because I'd just scored. I'm the type of player that, I've said before, I'm really good when I play off adrenaline.

"When I score, I normally don't have many bad games because I get into an untouchable mode of confidence. It makes me feel on top of the world. Especially in that moment, on that stage, I felt really good."

Gordon also said that Tuchel and the squad conducted a comprehensive review when they reconvened at St George's Park before their four-game UEFA Nations League slate during this international window.

He explained: "We had a meeting on the first day, which was important because we're probably best not kidding each other. It was a massive disappointment because we felt like we were going to win, or we felt in a really good place. So it was important to just get that out the way and move forwards.

"It was quite a positive meeting. The coach was just saying 'thank you' for a lot of things because, as far as the summer goes, it was the best of my life. I had some of the best experiences that I've ever had in that summer. So I couldn't be any more happy and proud.

"It was just a contrast in that moment. I've never felt better than when I scored that goal in the Argentina game and I've also never felt worse than 20 minutes later. So it was really important we got that out of the way.

"Being totally honest, I think any time you lose anything of value in life - whether it be a person or something like a match or anything you really want to have or win or anything of large value - you'll never be the same person.

"It leaves a scar, but that scar doesn't always have to be a negative one. You can be a better person for it. You can learn different things about the world, about yourself.

"So that's kind of the way I'm looking at it, and hopefully, me and the team will get better for it rather than the other way around."
